cards.explanation: The complaint is that Peter visited uncircumcised men and ate with them. The circumcised believers tell Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, “You visited uncircumcised men and ate with them.” Notice they don't say a word about the trip itself. It's about who he sat down with at the table. I think Peter felt that one, friends, because nobody likes being called out over who they ate with.

The answer is False. Peter stays. Acts 11:4 says Peter “…began and explained to them the whole sequence of events…” He doesn't dodge the question or head for the door. He lays the whole thing out, one piece at a time. When people take issue with you, bakers, a calm explanation beats a dramatic exit.

The answer is something like a large sheet. Peter says he was praying in Joppa and, in a trance, saw “…something like a large sheet being let down from heaven by its four corners…” Notice he says “something like.” He's describing what he saw as honestly as he can. And it came right down to him (Acts 11:5).

The voice tells Peter to get up and kill and eat. He tells the believers, “Then I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Get up, Peter, kill and eat.’” The voice calls him by name and gives a plain command. And there's the sheet full of animals right in front of him. I think Peter's jaw hit the floor.

His reason is that nothing impure has ever entered his mouth. Peter answers, “No, Lord,” and then says, “for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” He's honest about it, friends, even while talking to the Lord. Then the voice speaks again, and what it says changes the whole conversation (Acts 11:9).

The answer is True. Peter says, “But the voice spoke from heaven a second time, ‘Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.’” Notice the voice doesn't let his answer be the last word. It speaks again, plain and clear. I've had to hear things twice myself, bakers, and I never had a voice from heaven doing it.

The Spirit tells Peter to go with the three men without hesitation. Peter says, “The Spirit told me to accompany them without hesitation.” Three men show up at the door, and the Spirit says go, no dragging his feet. After the vision he'd just had, I bet that one clicked into place. And six brothers went along with him too.

The answer is True. Peter tells the believers that the man, Cornelius (Acts 10:1), told them how he had seen an angel standing in his house and saying, “Send to Joppa for Simon who is called Peter.” The angel gave Cornelius Peter's name. That's how a houseful of Gentiles ends up with an apostle at the door, friends.

It was just the same. Peter says the Holy Spirit fell upon them “…just as He had fallen upon us at the beginning.” He lines the two moments up with “just as.” A few verses later he calls it “…the same gift…” (Acts 11:17). There's no ranking in this story, bakers.

Peter asks who he was to hinder God's work. He says, “So if God gave them the same gift He gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to hinder the work of God?” He doesn't ask them to vote on it. He asks who he is to stand in the way. That's a humble thing to say, friends.

The answer is False. The text says, “When they heard this, they had no further objections…” Peter told them the whole sequence of events, and it settled things. The same people who took issue with him are the ones who stop objecting.

The believers in Jerusalem glorify God. The text says they “glorified God, saying, ‘So then, God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life.’” They went from objecting to praising, friends. And the praise is about what God did, not about who won the argument.
